strengths: Timely and relevant survey: it addresses trustworthiness, attribution, citation, and quotation for LLM-generated text, an increasingly important area in NLP.

The systematic mapping methodology is relatively transparent: it reports databases, a search string, inclusion criteria, and a final set of 134 papers, which makes the scope of the survey clearer than many ad hoc reviews.

The paper provides a broad and useful synthesis: it introduces a multi-dimensional taxonomy covering attribution approaches, LLM integration, citation characteristics, and tasks, and it also categorizes 300 evaluation metrics, 17 frameworks, 231 datasets, and 11 benchmarks.
The evaluation section is a valuable reference for the community, highlighting fragmentation in evaluation practices and the lack of standardized benchmarks.
The paper identifies open challenges and future directions, including parametric attribution, standardized evaluation, and explainable citations, which can guide subsequent work.
weaknesses: The search string is narrow: ("large language model" OR "llm") AND ("citation" OR "attribution" OR "quote"). It may miss relevant work that uses terms such as "grounded generation", "evidence-based generation", "provenance", "verifiability", "source attribution", or "retrieval-augmented generation" without using citation/attribution/quote in the title or abstract, undermining the "comprehensive" claim.

The survey does not report inter-annotator agreement or reliability metrics for screening and categorization. Annotation was split between two authors with joint decisions, but without quantified agreement, the reproducibility and consistency of the taxonomy are difficult to assess.

Reproducibility is limited: the annotated dataset is said to be available in a public Git repository, but no URL is provided in the manuscript, and there is no PRISMA-style flow diagram or detailed per-database search and exclusion counts.

The evaluation analysis is largely descriptive. It lists and categorizes metrics but does not critically appraise their validity, reliability, correlations, or practical trade-offs, nor does it provide clear guidance on which metrics or frameworks should be preferred under which conditions.

Some taxonomy categories contain very few papers (e.g., quote citation style with one paper, highlight gradient with two), which risks overfitting the taxonomy to isolated examples rather than identifying robust classes.

The data cutoff is February 2025, which may make the survey outdated by the time of ACL 2026. The rapid growth of the field means many relevant 2025–2026 papers are likely missing, and the claim that 86% of studies appeared after 2023 is based only on the authors' own filtered dataset.

The paper does not conduct a quality assessment or risk-of-bias appraisal of the included studies, which is typically expected in a systematic review or mapping study aiming to synthesize a research landscape.

strengths: Timely and comprehensive: the survey covers 134 papers, 300 evaluation metrics, 231 datasets, 17 frameworks, and 11 benchmarks, and releases an annotated dataset — a genuinely useful consolidation of a fast-growing, fragmented area (evidence-based text generation / attribution / citation / quotation).

Methodologically documented: it follows established systematic-mapping-study guidelines (Petersen et al., 2008), specifies a search string, queries nine databases, states inclusion criteria, and reports PRISMA-style counts (805 unique → 134 included), which makes the literature search largely traceable.

The proposed taxonomy is clear and operationally useful. Organizing the field along four dimensions (attribution approach, LLM integration, citation characteristics, task) and further decomposing attribution into seven approaches (pure LLM, data-centric, model-centric, post-retrieval, in-context, post-generation, in-generation) and citation characteristics into five axes helps unify inconsistent terminology (citation vs. attribution vs. quote).

The analysis of evaluation practices is a real contribution: the observation that 300 metrics exist but only two frameworks and two benchmarks are reused more than twice is a concrete, actionable diagnosis of the field's lack of standardization.

Well-organized and readable, with informative figures (taxonomy, evaluation-metric map, distribution plots) and a well-positioned related-work section that differentiates this survey from prior work (Li et al., 2023; Huang & Chang, 2024).
The discussion of open challenges (parametric attribution, standardized evaluation, explainable citations, human-evaluation variance) is relevant and points to concrete future directions.
weaknesses: No formal inter-annotator agreement or reliability statistic is reported. Annotation was split between the first two authors with only 'regular reviews' to resolve ambiguities. For a systematic review whose central artifacts are categorical counts, the absence of any IAA (e.g., Cohen's κ) is a meaningful methodological gap and limits confidence in reproducibility.

The search string — ("large language model" OR "llm") AND ("citation" OR "attribution" OR "quote") — is narrow. Relevant work using other common terms (e.g., grounding, faithfulness, provenance, verifiability, evidence) could be systematically missed, which may bias the counts and the claimed coverage.

Conceptual novelty is limited: the taxonomy largely extends and reorganizes dimensions already proposed by Huang & Chang (2024) and Li et al. (2023). The claim of being 'the first comprehensive survey dedicated to this paradigm' is somewhat strong given closely related recent surveys.

The analysis is predominantly descriptive (frequency counts and categorization) rather than critical or quantitative synthesis. There is little comparative assessment of which approaches actually work, how metrics correlate, or how performance has evolved — which would be the higher-value payoff of such a survey.
No risk-of-bias or study-quality appraisal of the included works is performed, which is a standard component of systematic reviews and would strengthen the reliability of the synthesis.

Some reported statistics (e.g., used in 75% of papers, attribute 62%, quote 13%) are not clearly traceable from the presented material, and the public Git repository is referenced without a visible URL/DOI or details on the annotation schema/guidelines in the main text.

Section structure/ordering (e.g., Section 4 'Research Landscape' appearing before Section 5's taxonomy, and the placement of the categorization scheme under Methodology) is slightly awkward and could be streamlined.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: evidence-based text generation with LLMs (attribution, citation, quotation) is central to trustworthiness and verifiability, and the survey provides a consolidated view of a fragmented field.

The methodology follows an established systematic mapping protocol (Petersen et al., 2008) with explicit research questions, a documented search string, inclusion criteria, and screening across nine literature databases, which is more disciplined than many narrative surveys.

The paper assembles a substantial and reusable resource: 134 annotated papers, ~300 evaluation metrics organized along seven dimensions and six methods, 231 datasets, 17 frameworks, and 11 benchmarks, with the annotated dataset released in a public Git repository.

The proposed taxonomy (attribution approach, LLM integration, citation characteristics, task) is clearly presented and organizes a genuinely heterogeneous literature into coherent categories that could help future work position itself.

The evaluation-metric section (Section 6) is the most valuable part of the paper, systematically mapping metric clusters (e.g., Citation NLI, ROUGE, RAGAS, G-Eval) to dimensions and methods, which is a useful reference for practitioners.
The authors correctly identify fragmentation in terminology and evaluation practice and differentiate their scope from prior surveys (Huang and Chang, 2024; Li et al., 2023).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central contribution: the taxonomy is largely adapted from prior work (Huang and Chang, 2024; Li et al., 2023; Schneider et al., 2022; Dziri et al., 2022), and the new dimensions (e.g., in-generation, in-context) are incremental refinements rather than a substantively new framework.

The search string is narrow — ("large language model" OR "llm") AND ("citation" OR "attribution" OR "quote") — and would plausibly miss highly relevant work using terminology such as "grounded," "evidence," "source," "verifiability," or "faithfulness." This undermines the strong comprehensiveness and "first comprehensive survey" claims.
The "first comprehensive survey" framing is overstated given multiple existing surveys on LLM attribution and citation (e.g., Zhang et al., 2023a; Li et al., 2023; Huang and Chang, 2024).

Methodological rigor of the review is under-documented: no inter-annotator agreement (e.g., Cohen's kappa) is reported for screening or categorization, and the PRISMA-style selection flow (805 to 134) is only summarized in a table, making reproducibility of inclusion decisions difficult to assess.

The paper is predominantly descriptive: Sections 5–6 catalog and count papers and metrics but provide little critical synthesis, quality appraisal of the surveyed work, or comparative insight; the discussion and future directions (Section 7) are generic ("need standardized evaluation," "explore hybrid approaches").

Some numerical claims are internally inconsistent or unclear — e.g., the counts shown in Figure 7 appear to sum well beyond the stated 300 metrics, and the definition of "framework" versus "benchmark" is fuzzy, with most frameworks/benchmarks used only once, limiting the utility of the summary.

Given the February 2025 data cutoff in a fast-moving area, many of the survey's conclusions risk becoming quickly outdated, and the authors do not discuss how the survey will be maintained beyond the Git repository.
The figures (especially Figure 4's taxonomy and Figure 7's metric grid) are dense and hard to read, reducing their practical value as a reference.

The work does not clearly articulate what actionable insights or new research questions emerge from the synthesis beyond identifying fragmentation; the impact on advancing the field is therefore uncertain.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated survey: it identifies and addresses a real gap (fragmented terminology and evaluation practices in evidence-based text generation with LLMs) and consolidates a rapidly growing literature (75% of the 134 papers published after 2023).

Methodologically rigorous for a survey: the authors follow the PRISMA protocol, report the search strings, databases queried (9 sources), inclusion criteria, deduplication numbers, and a sensitivity analysis showing the single primary search string is adequate (~4% additional relevant hits).

Reproducibility is strong: the annotated dataset of 134 papers, 300 metrics, and 231 datasets is released under an open license, and the paper reports Krippendorff's alpha for inclusion screening (1.0) and for taxonomy dimensions (0.73-1.00), with a clear multi-label annotation scheme.

The multidimensional, faceted taxonomy (attribution approach, citation characteristics, task, LLM integration) is genuinely useful and more granular than prior categorizations, introducing finer distinctions such as in-generation/in-context attribution and evidence-level granularity that could guide future work.

The evaluation analysis (300 metrics grouped into seven dimensions and six methods) and the resulting practical guidelines in Table 1, distinguishing 'core' vs. 'contextual' dimensions, provide actionable recommendations that are likely to be used by the community.

Clear presentation: informative figures (temporal trend bubble plots, distribution bars, taxonomy diagram, citation-style visualization) effectively communicate quantitative findings and make the survey easy to navigate.
weaknesses: As a survey, the paper's core contribution is descriptive synthesis rather than novel methods or new empirical evidence; the incremental novelty over closely related prior surveys/position papers (e.g., Huang & Chang 2024; Li et al. 2023a) is largely the broader scope and finer taxonomy, which reviewers may view as a modest technical contribution.

Several classification decisions remain subjective despite IAA reporting (e.g., how PURR is assigned to post-retrieval vs. post-generation; the labeling of 'core' vs. 'contextual' evaluation dimensions), and the proposed guidelines are asserted rather than validated empirically, so they are best treated as expert opinion.

Inter-annotator agreement for the parametric attribution dimension could not be computed because no such papers appeared in the annotated sample, leaving a gap in reliability evidence for the part of the taxonomy that the paper itself highlights as underexplored and important.

The literature search was conducted in February 2025 and restricted to English-language, publicly accessible sources; despite the sensitivity analysis, the fast-moving nature of the field means the corpus may already be dated, and proprietary/industry work is excluded.

While the survey notes fragmentation of evaluation, it does not itself attempt to unify or empirically compare metrics on shared data, so the practical impact is limited to guidance rather than demonstrated standardization; no quantitative meta-analysis of reported results across studies is attempted.

strengths: Provides the first comprehensive systematic survey dedicated to evidence-based text generation with LLMs, consolidating fragmented terminology and offering a unified multi-dimensional taxonomy spanning attribution approaches, citation characteristics, tasks, LLM integration, and evaluation.

Methodologically rigorous literature review: PRISMA-based identification/screening, nine databases, transparent inclusion criteria, sensitivity analysis for search robustness, and high inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha reported per dimension).

Substantial resource contribution: 134 annotated papers, 300 evaluation metrics, 19 frameworks, 11 benchmarks, 231 datasets, and a public GitHub repository, which supports reproducibility and reuse by the community.

Actionable synthesis: identifies trends, open challenges, and future directions (e.g., parametric/hybrid attribution, explainable citations, multimodal evidence, evaluation standardization) and provides practical evaluation guidelines distinguishing core and contextual dimensions.

Well-written and well-organized, with extensive appendices, useful summary tables/figures, and clear taxonomies that make the paper likely to serve as a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners.
weaknesses: The literature search was conducted in February 2025, but the field is evolving extremely quickly; by the time of publication, the survey may be substantially outdated, missing many papers from later in 2025 and 2026. This limits its long-term coverage and impact.

The primary search string ('citation' OR 'attribution' OR 'quote') is narrow relative to the broader space of grounding, verifiability, provenance, and source attribution. Although a sensitivity analysis found only 4% additional relevant studies, the query may still bias the corpus and taxonomy toward citation-centric terminology.

The review is restricted to English-language and publicly accessible papers, excluding non-English research, industry/proprietary work, and non-public sources. The paper acknowledges this, but it limits the representativeness of the claimed landscape.

No formal risk-of-bias or study-quality assessment is performed for the included papers, which is somewhat atypical for PRISMA-style systematic reviews and weakens the ability to weigh evidence quality across methods.

The taxonomy and evaluation guidelines are largely expert-driven and descriptive; they are not empirically validated beyond two annotators, and the core/contextual evaluation distinction, while useful, remains somewhat subjective.

The survey reports many statistics and trends but relatively limited critical, in-depth meta-analysis or adjudication of conflicting findings. It maps the field well but less often evaluates the comparative effectiveness of methods.

Some novelty framing is contestable: prior surveys exist on attribution, citation, hallucination, and retrieval-augmented generation. The paper distinguishes itself, but the 'first survey dedicated to this paradigm' claim could be softened.

As a survey with no new empirical experiments, the main-conference case rests heavily on synthesis quality and resource value; while strong, this leaves it closer to a Findings-style contribution than a technically novel main-conference paper.

strengths: The paper follows a PRISMA-inspired protocol with a documented search string, inclusion criteria, deduplication, and inter-annotator agreement (κ=1.0 for inclusion screening; macro-averaged κ for taxonomy dimensions), which makes the review process transparent and reproducible compared with many surveys.

It consolidates a large and fast-growing literature (134 papers) into a faceted taxonomy spanning attribution approach, citation characteristics, tasks, LLM integration, evaluation methods, and evaluation dimensions, and it releases an annotated dataset/repository.

The appendix and tables provide a useful reference for evaluation resources (300 metrics, 19 frameworks, 11 benchmarks, 231 datasets) and identify underexplored areas such as parametric attribution, multimodal evidence, and standardization of evaluation.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely descriptive: it maps and counts papers and metrics rather than critically synthesizing evidence, assessing study quality, or providing meta-analytic conclusions. Claims about trends, limitations, and future directions are therefore not strongly supported by the data presented.

The literature search is narrower and less current than the paper's framing implies: it relies on one title/abstract search string with limited adjacent terms, excludes non-English work, and has a February 2025 cutoff. The sensitivity analysis is not sufficient to establish comprehensive coverage across the full set of databases.

The proposed taxonomy overlaps with prior frameworks (e.g., Huang & Chang 2024; Li et al. 2023a), and the claim of being the first dedicated survey is not fully substantiated. Several taxonomy dimensions and the evaluation-metric classifications lack reported validation or reliability estimates.

Evaluation guidelines (core vs contextual dimensions) are presented without empirical validation showing that they improve comparability or that they are grounded in the surveyed evidence. The paper also does not analyze which methods or metrics actually perform well, limiting practical guidance for the ACL community.

The manuscript is dense and resource-heavy, but many takeaways are counts and distributions rather than actionable or evidence-based insights; the separate LLM-integration analysis is not clearly integrated into the taxonomy or evaluation recommendations.
